title: RFID Supply Chain Management — GS1 EPCIS 2.0 + DSCSA / EU FMD / FSMA 204 / EUDR / ESPR DPP
summary: On most enterprise rollouts, RFID supply chain management uses UHF RAIN RFID tags on items, cases and pallets to provide real-time visibility at every node — manufacturing, distribution centres, in-transit, retail stores, returns processing — and binds that visibility to the GS1 EPCIS 2.0 (ISO/IEC 19987:2021) event-sharing standard so trading partners, regulators and brand owners consume the same chain-of-custody record. RFID-enabled supply chains reduce shipment errors materially, cut receiving time substantially and enable same-day inventory accuracy that barcode-based systems cannot achieve, while satisfying DSCSA (US pharma), EU FMD (EU pharma), FSMA Section 204 (US food traceability), EUDR (EU deforestation regulation), EU 2024/1781 ESPR (Digital Product Passport) and US CBP C-TPAT chain-of-custody requirements.
heroPoints: End-to-end visibility. Track products from the factory floor through distribution, transit and retail with automated RFID reads at every handoff point.
95% fewer shipment errors. Automated RFID verification at packing and shipping catches mis-picks, wrong quantities and mislabeled cartons before they leave the facility.
80% faster receiving: portal readers scan an entire pallet of RFID-tagged cartons in seconds as it passes through the dock door, replacing manual barcode scanning.

brief.label: GS1 identifier scheme — what to encode
items: SGTIN-96 (Serialised Global Trade Item Number) — item-level encoding; combines GTIN with serial.
SGTIN-198 — pharma DSCSA / EU FMD requirement (longer serial range supports lot/batch + expiry).
SSCC-96 (Serial Shipping Container Code) — case + pallet level; required for ASN / EDI 856.
GRAI-96 (Global Returnable Asset Identifier) — reusable totes, IBCs, kegs, drums.
GIAI-96 (Global Individual Asset Identifier) — fixed assets in supply-chain visibility scope.
GLN (Global Location Number) — facility / building / dock-door identifier carried in EPCIS read events.
GS1 Digital Link 1.3 (ISO/IEC 18975:2023) — web-resolvable URL form for ESPR DPP convergence.
MIL-STD-130N IUID — defence supply-chain alternative to GS1.

brief.label: Regulatory carriers RFID supports
items: DSCSA (US pharmaceutical, effective 27 Nov 2024) — serialised item-level tracking + verification + suspect-product reporting via SGTIN-198.
EU FMD 2011/62/EU — Falsified Medicines Directive; serialisation + tamper-evidence + EMVS verification, in force since 9 Feb 2019.
FSMA Section 204 (US food, effective 20 Jan 2026) — Food Traceability List traceability rule; key data elements per CTE (Critical Tracking Event).
EUDR EU 2023/1115 (EU deforestation, effective 30 Dec 2025) — beef, soy, palm, cocoa, coffee, rubber, wood; Geographic origin claim per consignment.
ESPR EU 2024/1781 (EU Digital Product Passport) — textiles 2027, batteries 2027 (under EU 2023/1542), electronics 2028+.
MDR EU 2017/745 + IVDR — UDI requirements for medical devices supply chain.
WHO PQS prequalification — vaccine cold-chain RFID temperature-logger compliance.
GHS / REACH — hazardous substance chain-of-custody for chemicals supply chain.

brief.label: EPCIS event taxonomy
items: ObjectEvent — single object commissioning, observation, decommissioning at a single read point.
AggregationEvent — case-to-pallet, item-to-case association.
TransactionEvent — purchase order / shipping notice / receiving acknowledgment binding.
TransformationEvent — manufacturing / processing converting input objects to output objects (FSMA-relevant for food).
AssociationEvent — sensor-tag pairing (cold-chain logger to pallet).
Event vocabularies: bizStep (commissioning, packing, shipping, receiving, retail-selling, etc.), disposition (active, in-transit, in-progress, sellable, returned, destroyed).

Compliance avoidance value: DSCSA non-compliance penalties up to $10K per violation; EU FMD up to €50K per batch; FSMA 204 penalties scaling per FDA guidance.

Stage 5 — Visibility platform + EPCIS broker selection (atma.io / IBM Sterling / GS1 ONE Record / TraceLink / Optel / Antares Vision / rfxcel / custom).
Stage 6 — Pilot one node + one trading-partner edge for end-to-end validation.
Stage 7 — Production ramp + multi-node + multi-partner rollout.
Stage 8 — Operate + audit + extend to additional product groups + regulatory carriers.

sections.title: RFID at each supply chain node

before: Barcode scanning at every handoff — line-of-sight required, manual operation, slow.
EDI 856 ASN sent at shipment level only — no in-transit visibility, no item-level granularity.
Receiving discrepancies surface days after delivery — chargebacks negotiated post-fact.
DSCSA / FMD / FSMA 204 compliance evidence stitched together from disparate systems.
Trading-partner visibility partial — buyer sees ASN, not actual item-level state.
Reverse logistics blind — returns processed by manual SKU lookup.
after: RFID portal + handheld reads at every node — non-line-of-sight, automatic, near-instant.
EPCIS 2.0 events shared in near-real-time — item / case / pallet level granularity at every observation.
Receiving discrepancies caught at dock-door portal — flagged before shipment leaves origin.
Compliance evidence pulled directly from EPCIS broker — DSCSA / FMD / FSMA 204 / EUDR / ESPR DPP audit-ready.
Trading-partner full chain-of-custody — buyer + regulator see same event stream.
Reverse logistics automated — returned items identified by RFID, routed to disposition rule.

sections.title: RFID tags for supply chain applications
bullets: Item-level source tags. UHF RFID labels applied at the point of manufacture (garment source tags, product labels) for end-to-end item tracking from factory to consumer.
Case-level labels: RFID shipping labels on cartons encoding SSCC (Serial Shipping Container Code) for automated case-level receiving and inventory management.
Pallet-level tags: high-read-range UHF tags on pallets for dock-door portal reads, cross-dock routing and warehouse zone tracking.
Reusable container tags: durable UHF hard tags on totes, bins and returnable transport items (RTIs) for closed-loop container tracking and pooling management.
Seal and tamper tags. RFID-enabled tamper-evident seals for container doors, pharmaceutical shipments and high-value cargo requiring chain-of-custody verification.

dataHighlight.heading: Regulatory cliff — five major mandates inside 18 months
dataHighlight.text: Five regulatory carriers force RFID supply-chain visibility into global enterprise programmes inside an 18-month window: DSCSA (US pharma, effective 27 Nov 2024 — already active), EUDR (EU deforestation, effective 30 December 2025), FSMA Section 204 (US food traceability, effective 20 January 2026), EU 2023/1542 Battery Passport (effective 18 February 2027), and EU 2024/1781 ESPR Digital Product Passport for textiles + leather + footwear (delegated act expected 2026, mandatory 2027). All five align on GS1 EPCIS 2.0 (ISO/IEC 19987:2021) event sharing + GS1 Digital Link 1.3 (ISO/IEC 18975:2023) URL structure as the data carrier — meaning a single EPCIS-compliant RFID supply-chain programme can satisfy all five regulators with shared cryptographic + provenance infrastructure. Programme economics: enterprise rollouts at $250K–$5M spend typically pay back inside 12–18 months on retail apparel + 18–36 months on pharma compliance-driven; secondary savings span 95% shipment-error reduction, 80% receiving-time cut, 30–50% labour reduction, 10–20% inventory-carrying-cost cut, and 15–30% shrinkage reduction.

faq.question: What is the ROI timeline for RFID supply chain deployment?
faq.answer: Most organizations achieve positive ROI within 12-18 months. The primary savings come from reduced labor for receiving and counting (30-50% reduction), fewer shipment errors and chargebacks (90-95% reduction), decreased inventory carrying costs (10-20% reduction through better visibility), and reduced shrinkage and loss (15-30% improvement).

faq.question: Do we need to tag every item or just cases and pallets?
faq.answer: It depends on your visibility goals. Case-and-pallet tagging provides facility-level and shipment-level visibility at lower cost. Item-level tagging provides the richest data (individual product tracking from factory to point of sale) and is most valuable for high-value goods, apparel and products requiring serialization. Many companies start with case-level and expand to item-level over time.

faq.question: Which RFID encoding standard should we use for supply chain?
faq.answer: GS1 EPC (Electronic Product Code) standards are the industry default. Use SGTIN-96 for item-level encoding, SSCC-96 for case/pallet-level encoding, GRAI-96 for reusable assets, and SGTIN-198 for pharma DSCSA / EU FMD where lot+expiry must be carried. These standards ensure interoperability across trading partners, retailers and 3PL providers. Proud Tek encodes tags in any GS1 EPC format during production.

faq.question: How does GS1 EPCIS 2.0 fit alongside RFID hardware?
faq.answer: GS1 EPCIS 2.0 (ISO/IEC 19987:2021) is the event-sharing standard that lets trading partners + regulators consume the same chain-of-custody record from your RFID reads. Your reader fleet captures Object / Aggregation / Transaction / Transformation / Association events; an EPCIS broker (GS1 ONE Record, IBM Sterling Supply Chain Insights, atma.io by Avery Dennison, TraceLink, Optel, Antares Vision, rfxcel) publishes those events outward to subscribers. Without EPCIS the reads are operationally useful internally but invisible to regulators or trading partners.

faq.question: Which regulatory mandates does RFID supply-chain visibility help satisfy?
faq.answer: DSCSA (US pharmaceutical, effective 27 Nov 2024) requires serialised item-level tracking via SGTIN-198. EU FMD has been in force since Feb 2019 with EMVS verification. FSMA Section 204 (US food, effective 20 Jan 2026) introduces the Food Traceability List with critical tracking events. EUDR EU 2023/1115 (EU deforestation, effective 30 Dec 2025) requires per-consignment geographic-origin claims for forest-products and selected commodities. EU 2024/1781 ESPR Digital Product Passport requires GS1 Digital Link URL carriers for textiles + leather (2027), batteries (2027 under EU 2023/1542) and electronics (2028+). RFID + EPCIS satisfies all of these as a single shared infrastructure.
